Distributed training across many GPUs achieves consistency by assuming all workers perform floating-point arithmetic at effectively the same rate and precision — but thermal throttling silently violates this assumption by causing individual GPUs to drop clock speeds mid-computation, changing the timing and sometimes the order of floating-point operations. Because floating-point arithmetic is not associative, reordering reductions (e.g., AllReduce gradient aggregations) across thermally heterogeneous workers produces numerically different gradient values each step, and these differences don't cancel — they accumulate. The central question is whether this drift is bounded and benign, or whether it compounds across thousands of steps into measurably worse model convergence, gradient corruption, or silent training divergence that looks superficially like a learning rate problem. A beginner sees throttling as a throughput issue (slower iteration time) and stops there; an expert worries about the asymmetry — that a throttled GPU may be computing a subtly different gradient than its peers, contributing a systematically biased signal to the parameter update, and that this bias may correlate with model regions or batch content in non-random ways that evade standard loss curve diagnostics. The deeper concern is that commodity clusters have no thermal uniformity guarantees, so throttling patterns vary by chassis position, ambient temperature, and workload history, making the drift stochastic in ways that are nearly impossible to reproduce for debugging.

In a ring-AllReduce (as implemented in NCCL, the dominant backend for PyTorch and TensorFlow distributed), divergence first becomes observable at the partial reduce-scatter phase, where each GPU accumulates a contiguous chunk of the gradient buffer by summing contributions from its ring neighbors sequentially. Because the summation order is determined by ring topology and message arrival timing — and a throttled GPU delays its send, causing its neighbor to receive chunks out of the expected temporal order or to proceed with a locally reordered partial sum — the floating-point error enters at the very first addition in that chain. This matters enormously for mitigation because the reduce-scatter output feeds directly into the allgather phase with no subsequent correction opportunity; whatever numerical error exists in the scattered chunks gets broadcast faithfully to all workers, meaning a single throttled node's drift gets replicated cluster-wide rather than averaged away. (2021) on deterministic distributed training quantifies that even without throttling, ring-AllReduce across 64 GPUs accumulates O(n·ε_machine) error per reduction where n is ring length — throttling adds a time-varying perturbation on top of this baseline. The location matters because mitigation strategies diverge sharply depending on the entry point: if drift enters at reduce-scatter, you can address it with compensated summation (Kahan summation) or by switching to a tree-AllReduce topology that has fewer sequential additions, but these remedies are ineffective if you wrongly diagnose the problem as a gradient clipping or batch normalization issue downstream.

NCCL's synchronization barrier does enforce that all GPUs reach the same logical step before the AllReduce result is consumed by the optimizer — but this is a completion barrier, not an ordering barrier, and conflating the two is a precise mistake beginners make. The barrier guarantees that every GPU has a complete gradient buffer before the next forward pass begins; it says nothing about the order in which partial sums were accumulated within the reduce-scatter phase on each GPU. The numerical damage therefore comes not from reordering across the barrier but from within-chunk summation order variability on individual GPUs: a throttled GPU running at reduced clock speed may execute its local CUDA reduction kernel with different instruction-level interleaving than a full-speed peer, and CUDA's parallel reduction kernels (including those NCCL calls internally) are explicitly documented by Nvidia as non-deterministic by default because warp scheduling under thermal load is not fixed. This is confirmed by Reproducibility in Deep Learning (Zhuang et al., 2022) and PyTorch's own determinism documentation, which notes that torch.use_deterministic_algorithms(True) incurs 10–20% throughput overhead specifically because it forces serialized reductions to eliminate this warp-schedule sensitivity. The implication is sharp: the barrier actually masks the problem diagnostically, because every worker reports a "complete" gradient that looks well-formed, while the numerical content of that gradient has already been corrupted by non-deterministic local reduction on the throttled node before the barrier was ever reached.

The detectable signature is therefore a persistent directional bias in the gradient second moment — specifically, if you log per-layer gradient variance across workers using a framework hook (PyTorch's register_hook on parameters), a throttled worker will show elevated variance on layers whose weight matrices are large enough that their reduction chunks land disproportionately on that worker's ring segment, and this elevation will be stable across steps rather than fluctuating, distinguishing it from batch noise. At the weight update level, the signature appears as layer-wise learning rate effective drift: Adam's second moment estimator v_t will absorb the bias as artificially inflated gradient variance for specific parameter blocks, causing Adam to reduce the effective step size for those parameters — meaning throttling-induced drift manifests not as divergence but as selective underfitting in the layers whose chunks route through the hot GPU.

The key construction constraint is that sequences must be naturalistic rather than artificially frequency-filtered, because stripping high-frequency function words to hit a frequency target destroys the syntactic context that makes perplexity meaningful — instead, select documents from domains that naturally produce mid-frequency vocabulary: technical journalism, mid-tier Wikipedia articles, and domain-specific corpora like PubMed abstracts work well because they use specialized but repeatedly-appearing terminology. The detection signal should be computed not as raw perplexity but as the ratio of canary perplexity to a high-frequency control set (top decile tokens, ~100 sequences) evaluated simultaneously — this ratio is dimensionless and cancels out learning rate schedule effects, making it sensitive specifically to differential embedding quality rather than global training progress. A ratio drift of more than 4–6% relative to the moving average of the previous 10 checkpoints should trigger an alert, based on the observation that normal training produces stable perplexity ratios across frequency buckets (variance typically under 2% between adjacent checkpoints in stable runs like those reported in the Chinchilla scaling paper). The canary should be frozen at the start of training — never updated, never resampled — so it functions as a true fixed probe; this also means you can precompute token frequency assignments once and cache them, making per-checkpoint overhead purely the forward pass cost with no preprocessing penalty.
